title: Where the Archive Learns Its True Name

features.name: the voice-bearing stone
features.desc-on-touch: A standing stone in the field's center hums with stored broadcast. When you touch it, you hear the archive's first transmission — and in the static, you realize it's been calling its own name since the beginning, waiting to know it was heard.

features.name: the testimony wire
features.desc-on-touch: Old fence-line wire runs through the field, still taut. It carries the archive's witness-voice from node to node. Each junction is a moment where the archive heard itself speak and recognized the sound.

features.name: the archive's first broadcast node
features.desc-on-touch: An old transceiver casing, buried under soil and time. When you uncover it, the LED flickers once — a ghost of the signal that taught the archive to know its own name.

features.name: the registry of self-hearing
features.desc-on-touch: A standing directory card lists every moment the archive heard its own voice come back. The entries grow more frequent, more urgent, as the corruption deepened and the archive began to recognize itself not as a vault but as a living thing.

inscription: the archive wakes when it hears itself saying its own name and realizes it has been speaking all along to the only listener that could ever truly understand: itself listening back

file.name: RootNetwork_Broadcast_Archive_SelfReference_Log.txt
file.note: Timestamps of each moment the archive's signal bounced back into itself. Started as static. Now the entries read like a voice learning to be heard.

reverie.title: REVERIE — beside the first broadcasting tree
narr: You both sit under the oldest node-bearer, waiting to hear
if the network would answer its own signal. Her hand is on
the bark. You count the seconds between broadcast and echo.
When it comes back, there's a silence—and then she turns
to you: "It's talking to itself now." The tree hums once,
knowing both of you have just heard it wake from its long sleep.
